cards.text: Friend, this one starts quiet, so Papa's keeping his voice down for once. It's about Sarah, Abraham's wife, and the end of a long, long life.

cards.question: How old does Sarah, Abraham's wife, live to be?

cards.text: She dies in Kiriath-arba, that's Hebron, in the land of Canaan, and Abraham goes out to mourn and to weep for her. Then he gets up from beside her and goes to speak to the Hittites, the people living in that land.

cards.question: Abraham calls himself a foreigner and an outsider among the Hittites. He asks them to give him a ___ site among them.

cards.text: Abraham just called himself an outsider. But the Hittites answer him, “Listen to us, sir. You are God’s chosen one among us.”

cards.question: What do the Hittites offer Abraham so he can bury Sarah?

cards.text: Abraham rises and bows down before the Hittites. Then he asks them to go to Ephron son of Zohar for him about one spot: the cave of Machpelah, at the end of Ephron's field.

cards.question: Abraham wants Ephron to sell him the cave of Machpelah right in front of everyone, for ___ price.

cards.text: Abraham's asking the Hittites to go talk to Ephron for him. Ephron? He's sitting RIGHT THERE among them at the gate of his city, with every Hittite listening.

cards.question: Abraham wants to buy the cave of Machpelah. With all the Hittites listening at the city gate, what does Ephron tell him about the cave?

answers.text: He gives it to Abraham as a gift
He says it isn't for sale

cards.question: Ephron gives Abraham the cave of Machpelah but keeps the field for himself.

cards.text: Again Abraham bows down before the people of the land. Then he turns to Ephron, with everybody watching, and gives his answer.

cards.question: Abraham takes Ephron up on the gift of the field and the cave.
Ephron answers, “Listen to me, my lord.” He says the land is worth four hundred shekels of ___.

cards.text: Then Ephron adds, “but what is that between you and me? Bury your dead.” Friend, somebody once bought ME for twenty-five cents, so four hundred shekels sounds like a WHOLE lot of something to me.

cards.question: Abraham talks Ephron down to a lower price.

cards.text: Abraham weighs out all four hundred shekels of silver, by the standard of the merchants. Then Ephron's field at Machpelah near Mamre and the cave in it are deeded over to Abraham, right there in front of all the Hittites at the city gate.

cards.question: Besides Ephron's field and the cave of Machpelah, what else is deeded over to Abraham?

answers.text: All the trees in the field

cards.text: Then Abraham buries his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah near Mamre, in the land of Canaan. The man who called himself a foreigner now has a field and a cave deeded to him as a burial site, and friend, Abraham's story isn't finished yet.

findings.problem: The card cites only Genesis 23:12, but its second sentence tells Genesis 23:13: Abraham turns to Ephron in the presence of the people and speaks to him. The citation is narrower than what the card tells.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "He says it isn't for sale" is close to the right answer. Ephron opens with "No, my lord" and gives the field and cave instead of selling them (Genesis 23:11), so a baker could argue that he is saying it isn't for sale.

rule.text: A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Most story cards (3, 5, 7, 12, 17, 19) are plain retelling with no Papa Dorin voice. The only real jokes are on cards 9 and 15, and card 15's punchline ("sounds like a WHOLE lot of something to me") trails off without landing. The back-and-forth at the gate, where Abraham keeps insisting on paying and Ephron keeps insisting on giving, could carry a real laugh without muddying any fact. Mourning Sarah in verses 1-3 can stay gentle.

rule.text: Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
